transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-10-20
Start: 16:30 PT
Duration: 48 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Lucas Ford (Redwood SE), Ravi Patel (Helios), Nora Li (Helios SRE), Ben Ortiz (Helios Product)

Summary:
Quick weekly POC check-in focusing on Dedicated sizing for upcoming holiday-style surge test. Reviewed initial metrics from last week's pilot run, discussed autoscale policy knobs (min pool, burst lanes, grace period), warm-pool strategies, and fallback behavior to hosted tiers. Agreed next steps and owners.

Topics:
- Observed latency/queue behavior during 2x weekend load test
- Autoscale-trigger thresholds and cooldowns
- Burst capacity lanes and pre-warming strategy
- Regional routing and per-customer concurrency caps
- Security/SSO/KMS note for Dedicated pilot

Transcript Body:
[00:00] Maya: okay everyone, thanks for joining. We got about 48 minutes, um, we wanted to focus on sizing and the surge prep for your 11/27 campaign, correct?
[00:12] Ravi: yeah that's right. 11/27 is our internal sale — think black friday lite — we need to be sure the POC Dedicated path can handle 2 to 3x typical peak for a 90 minute window.
[00:25] Lucas: right. last week's run hit, uh, a couple of interesting points. p50 looked fine, p95 spiked to about 1.2 seconds for generation-only endpoints and the queue began growing when token-rate exceeded 12k tokens per second.
[00:42] Nora: yes, we saw a sustained queue depth of 8-12 requests for about three minutes during the ramp, which caused cold-start-ish scheduling delays, I think partly because the warm pool was too small.
[00:55] Ben: and just to call out product concerns — we need deterministic tail latency under 1 second for high-priority orders, otherwise we'll route users to lightweight fallback flows.
[01:08] Maya: good note. so the main levers we can tune are: min_active_gpus for dedicated pool, burst_pool_size, autoscale_cooldown, and the warm-pool pre-warm window. also prefix/KV cache hit rates matter for repeat queries.
[01:28] Lucas: i ran some sim numbers: if you increase warm_pool to 20% of expected concurrency and set a burst lane of 2 GPUs for 15 minutes pre-warm, we see the p95 drop ~30% in sims. but that assumes model quantization to int8 and tokenization staying within 512 tokens average.
[01:45] Ravi: our average is 280 tokens but peak tends to have longer contexts up to 1024 for personalized messages, so how sensitive is the kernel selection to that?
[01:56] Lucas: it's sensitive — memory footprint and KV cache both increase linearly with sequence length. for 1024 tokens, per-request GPU memory use jumps and that reduces the number of concurrent lanes. we can use a hybrid model variant with half-precision and a smaller context window for high-priority paths.
[02:12] Nora: can you remind me about fallback? if Dedicated saturates do we automatically fall back to hosted nodes? we want to avoid failed requests.
[02:20] Maya: yes, you can configure a routing policy. current POC config falls back to Redwood Hosted 'standard' cluster with a slightly higher latency budget but guaranteed capacity. we can also set per-customer concurrency caps to prevent noisy neighbors.
[02:34] Ben: what about throttling? we prefer graceful degradation — return a short answer or a cached snippet instead of full generation if latency exceeds threshold.
[02:44] Lucas: that's handled at the application layer ideally — Redwood can surface metrics and token-level budget signals, but you'd need a routing rule: if queue > N or p95 > T, route to cached/shortflow endpoint. we can demo a rule.
[02:58] Ravi: looking at costs — is it cheaper to keep a warm pool vs allow short bursts and pay preemptive burst rates? our finance team will want estimates.
[03:06] Maya: good question. cost math depends on burst duration and percent of time warm pool is utilized. our Optimize tool has a workbook; Lucas will attach the workbook showing break-even point at about 12 minutes of sustained burst for your traffic profile.
[03:22] Lucas: right — i'll include 'warm_pool cost vs on-demand burst' chart. also recommend enabling continuous batching for high concurrency endpoints — it reduces per-token cost but can add a small batching latency tradeoff.
[03:36] Nora: last run we saw about 72% GPU util on the long-run but during spikes single-GPU machines hit 95% and then queued. is there a recommended GPU mix? a few A10G-style instances for steady traffic and a couple A100 or H100 for burst?
[03:50] Lucas: we usually recommend homogenous pools for predictability; however a tiered pool works: dedicated steady pool (A10G equivalent) for baseline, and short-lived high-power burst pool (A100/H100) if you need low tail latency on big context requests. Redwood routing will prefer compatible model variants when moving traffic to smaller GPUs.
[04:08] Ben: we have a compliance ask — SOC 2 plus audit logs for any data touching the Dedicated cluster. is that ready for the POC?
[04:16] Maya: yes we included the audit-log sample in the security packet last week; Dedicated supports KMS integration and logs are exportable to your SIEM. i'll resend the doc.
[04:25] Ravi: great. also SSO and RBAC — can we lock down who can change autoscale policies?
[04:31] Maya: yep, RBAC for console and API keys, with SSO/SAML mapping to roles. SE and config change events are recorded.
[04:38] Nora: on the technical side, for the 2x test you suggested earlier, what autoscale thresholds should we set?
[04:45] Lucas: for starters: min_active_gpus = baseline to handle 1.2x; scale_up when queue_length > 5 for more than 30s; scale_up_step = +2 GPUs; cooldown = 120s; and pre-warm trigger at T-15 minutes for the expected peak window. these numbers are tunable.
[05:02] Ravi: can we make the scale up step smaller, like +1, to reduce overshoot?
[05:06] Lucas: sure, +1 gives tighter control but slower ramp; with pre-warm you probably want larger steps to absorb sudden ramp. depends on your traffic slope.
[05:16] Ben: we ran a simulation that showed if ramp happens inside 3 minutes, we need at least +3 steps or a pre-warm.
[05:24] Maya: action item — Lucas will provide two recommended policies: conservative (+1 steps) and aggressive (+2/+3 steps) with cost delta.
[05:31] Lucas: noted. also worth calling out burst lanes: they are immutable for the test window — you reserve GPU capacity that doesn't drop below X during the window. it's good for guaranteed tail-latency.
[05:45] Nora: how does billing for burst lanes work? is it a separate commit or pay-as-you-go?
[05:50] Maya: for POC we can do temporary reserved burst lanes billed as metered usage; for production there is a reserved commit option with discount. I'll put options in the workbook.
[05:59] Ravi: regarding metrics — i'd like a dashboard with p50/p95/p99, queue depth, gpu utilization per pool, token/sec, and cold-start counts. can you ship a Grafana link or dashboard JSON?
[06:12] Lucas: yes — we'll share a curated dashboard and also the alert rules (p95 > threshold, queue > threshold).
[06:20] Ben: fine. testing plan?
[06:23] Maya: propose: 1) Redwood generates load scripts (we'll send JMeter/k6 flavors), 2) Helios shares traffic histograms, 3) we run a 2-hour run including 2x and a short 4x spike, 4) runbook includes rollback and fallback validation.
[06:41] Ravi: timeline works, can we do the run on Wed 10/29?
[06:44] Maya: yes, we penciled that in. we'll confirm times.
[06:47] Nora: one more question on model variants — during burst can we fall back to a smaller model that has faster latency but slightly lower quality?
[06:56] Lucas: absolutely. routing policy supports model-family fallbacks; you'll want to set an acceptance threshold for quality. Redwood's evaluate hooks can precompute a quality-vs-cost table for common prompts.
[07:08] Ben: curious about KV cache behavior — does it persist across pools or only per GPU instance? we saw cache misses during failovers.
[07:16] Lucas: KV cache is local to the runtime instance; when routing moves to a different machine the cache warms slowly. for high cache-hit workloads we recommend sticky routing using session affinity or a shared cache layer. we'll include tradeoffs in the workbook.
[07:32] Nora: ok. in terms of security during the load test — we will need to run test traffic through our VPC peering. any special egress or firewall rules?
[07:41] Maya: Redwood's private connectors will need the following ports — we'll send a checklist. also note egress quotas might limit multi-region bursts; we'll work with you to validate.
[07:52] Ravi: perfect.
[07:54] Maya: recap: Lucas creates load scripts + two autoscale policies, Maya sends burst-sizing workbook and security checklist, Helios shares traffic histograms and confirms egress quotas; we run the 2-hour surge test on 10/29. follow-up to finalize Dedicated commit 11/03.
[08:10] Ben: sounds good.
[08:12] Nora: thanks all.
[08:15] Maya: i'll share minutes and action items. thanks everyone.

Notes about transcript quality: automated transcription had minor mislabels (Speaker 2/3 mixed with names), a few technical terms were mistranscribed (A100 vs 'A one hundred'), and timestamps are approximate.
